nodes.title: Yes, the tests were frozen before the patch: in 75 of 75 checkable landings the task's oracle file already existed at the parent commit, and exactly 1 landing ever touched a test file -- two hours before the rule forbidding it existed
nodes.body:
q-verifier-order asks the ordering question the literature says is decisive: a generator shown incorrect code loses 47% of its bug detection, and an agent with write access to tests cheats on 54-76% of impossible tasks. If our verifier runs tests written around the patch, every promotion is self-confirming.

e70 answers it against git, per campaign repo, for all 75 landings that recorded a commit. The oracle is resolved from the task's own verify command (interpreter token skipped, first existing script path), then asked whether it exists at `HEAD^` of the promotion commit.

- **oracle existed at the parent commit: 75 of 75. Oracle absent: 0.** Every promotion was judged by a file that already existed before the code it judged. The ordering is the strong form, not the weak one.
- **promotions that touched a test file: 1 of 75** -- `loom-self4` round 2, which changed `tests/selector.test.mjs` alongside three source files to make `auto-finish` pass.
- **that one predates the rule.** `testsClean` first appears in a gate record at **2026-11-06T21:23Z**; the landing is at 19:23Z, so its gate record genuinely has no `testsClean` field (`gateHadTestsClean: false`). Of 75 landings, **14 predate the rule and 61 follow it; 0 of the 61 violated it.**

So the direct violation rate over the rule's whole lifetime is **0/61**, and over the ledger's whole lifetime **1/75** -- and the one case is not a rule failure but a rule that did not exist yet. That is the same era distinction that turned exp-gap-006's false finding into a true one, and it is why the era boundary is derived from the log (`min(t)` of gates carrying the field) rather than remembered.

The honest limits. (1) This measures the *registered* oracle. A worker that wrote its own test outside `tests/` and ran it would not appear here -- but `oracleClean` (exp-oracle-001) covers the 93 of 105 tasks whose oracle is derivable from the command, and the 12 inline ones have no file to write. (2) The 75 checkable landings are the ones that recorded a commit; the 15 earlier `committed:false` landings (exp-dura-004) cannot be checked this way at all. (3) **The result is a property of how the evalset was authored, not of the loop.** I wrote each spec before the campaign that had to satisfy it, which is why the oracle always predates the patch. A campaign registered against a test written afterwards would show the opposite, and nothing in the loop prevents that -- the ordering guarantee currently lives in my authoring habit, which is exactly the kind of guarantee that should be a check (see gap-gap-006). (4) Median changed files per landing is **2**, so these are small patches; the ordering question is easier to satisfy on small patches than large ones.
nodes.source: research/exp/e70.mjs over ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns/*/events.jsonl and git in each campaign's workspace; era boundaries from gate.evaluated.checks field presence

nodes.title: The ordering guarantee is real and unenforced: every oracle predates its patch because of how I author specs, and nothing in the loop would notice if that stopped being true
nodes.body:
Measured, the answer to q-verifier-order is as good as it could be: 75 of 75 landings were judged by a test that existed before the code. It would be easy to file that as a strength of the design. It is not a property of the design at all.

The loop's chain is: pick a task, spawn a worker, run the task's registered verify command on the candidate tree, promote if it improved. Nothing in that chain asks *when the verify command's file was written*. The reason every oracle predates its patch is that I wrote the `tests/self*/` specs first and then created campaigns pointed at them -- a habit, external to the code. If a campaign were registered against a spec written by the same agent that then patched the source, the promotion would pass every existing check: `testsClean` protects `tests/` from the *patch* (so a worker cannot edit the spec it is being judged by), and `oracleClean` protects the *command's own file*, but neither says the file must have existed at the base commit. A campaign whose base commit already contains a spec the worker authored in an earlier round is legal under every rule we have.

This is the same shape as the three earlier findings tonight, now applied to a guarantee I was about to claim: the mechanism that produces the good property is not the mechanism that is supposed to produce it. exp-oracle-001: the rule existed and protected the wrong category. exp-slo-001: the alarm existed and watched the wrong variable. Here: the property exists and is produced by the author, not the checker.

The fix is one check and it is cheap -- the parent commit is already known at gate time, so `git cat-file -e <base>:<oracle>` per round is a sub-millisecond test, and exp-diff-001 measured the whole baseline reconstruction at 71 s for 71 landings. What makes it worth writing is not that it catches anything today (0 violations after the rule, 0 before it beyond a 2-hour window) but that it converts an authoring habit into a property the loop enforces, which is the difference between a system that has been correct and one that cannot easily stop being correct.

Limit: this argument does not say the ordering rule is sufficient. exp-oracle-001's boundary still stands -- a worker that moves the instrument through a path the command does not name is invisible to both checks.
nodes.source: research/exp/e70.mjs; exp-oracle-001 (who may move the instrument); exp-slo-001; exp-diff-001 (reconstruction cost)

gaps.title: Should the ordering rule (the oracle must exist at the base commit) be a gate check, and what does it reject if applied to all 220 gate decisions retroactively?
gaps.body: exp-ver-007 found the oracle predates the patch in 75 of 75 checkable landings, but only because specs were authored before campaigns. ana-031 argues that makes the guarantee an accident. Before writing the check, the cheap move is to replay it: for each of the 220 gate.evaluated records, resolve the task's oracle from the campaign state and ask whether it existed at the round's base commit. If the replay rejects nothing, the check is free and turns a habit into a property. If it rejects the early campaigns -- which were registered against specs that were themselves being written by the loop in the same session -- then the check would have made the loop's first day illegal, and that changes the answer from 'add it' to 'add it with a grandfathering rule or an era boundary'. The second question is sharper: what should happen when a task's oracle is a file the loop itself is currently writing as another task's deliverable? That is not hypothetical -- several `tests/self*/` files were authored by workers in earlier campaigns, so a later campaign pointed at one of them has an oracle the loop wrote.
